nodes.summary: Given an assignment $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ of booleans to the variables and the list $v = (v_0, \dots, v_{k-1})$ of the values of the gates evaluated so far, an input index $r$ resolves to $x_r$ if $r < n$, to $v_{r-n}$ if $n \le r < n + k$, and to false if $r \ge n + k$.
nodes.title: Resolving a circuit input

nodes.summary: CIRCUIT SAT is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $s$ exactly when $s$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of circuit-satisfiability instances, to an instance that is well formed and satisfiable. Bitstrings that fail to decode are rejected.
nodes.title: The CIRCUIT SAT decision problem

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, G)$ is satisfiable when there is an assignment $x \in \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}^n$ of booleans to the $n$ variables such that the evaluation of the circuit $G$ under $x$ has a last gate value and that value is true. In particular an instance with no gates is not satisfiable.
nodes.title: Satisfiable circuit instances

nodes.summary: An instance of circuit satisfiability is a pair $(n, G)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a finite list $G$ of gates, each gate a triple $(o, a, b)$ of natural numbers: an operation code $o$, a first input $a$ and a second input $b$.
nodes.title: Circuit-satisfiability instances

nodes.summary: The CIRCUIT SAT decision problem on bitstrings belongs to the class NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
nodes.title: CIRCUIT SAT is NP-complete

nodes.summary: Given an assignment of booleans to the variables and a list of gates $g_1, \dots, g_m$, circuit evaluation returns the list $(v_1, \dots, v_m)$ of gate values, where $v_k$ is the value of the gate $g_k$ under the assignment and the earlier values $(v_1, \dots, v_{k-1})$.
nodes.title: Evaluating a circuit

nodes.summary: Let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be an assignment of booleans to the variables and $v$ the list of values of the earlier gates. An input index $r$ resolves to $x_r$ if $r < n$, and otherwise to $v_{r-n}$, or to false if that entry does not exist. The value of a gate $(o, a, b)$ is the conjunction of the resolved inputs $a$ and $b$ if $o = 0$, their disjunction if $o = 1$, the negation of the resolved input $a$ if…
nodes.title: Value of a gate

nodes.summary: For a wire that refers to one of $n$ inputs or one of $g$ gates, its position in $\{0, \dots, n + g - 1\}$ is $k$ if it is input $k$ and $n + j$ if it is gate $j$, so the inputs come first and the gates follow.
nodes.title: Certificate position of a wire

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output, and let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be truth values on which the output of $c$ under the Boolean interpretation is true. Let $b$ be the array $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}, v_0, \dots, v_{s-1})$, where $v_j$ is the value of gate $j$ of $c$ on input $x$. Then $b$ has length $n + s$ and the Boolean certificate verifier accepts $b$.
nodes.title: Completeness of the Boolean certificate verifier

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output, and let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ be an array of truth values, where an entry at a position at or beyond $m$ is read as false and the position of a wire is $k$ for input $k$ and $n + j$ for gate $j$. The Boolean certificate verifier accepts $b$ if and only if $m = n + s$, for every gate $j < s$ the Boolean interpretation of…
nodes.title: Characterization of accepted certificates

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output. The Boolean certificate verifier accepts some array of at most $n + 2s$ truth values if and only if there are truth values $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ on which the output of $c$ under the Boolean interpretation is true.
nodes.title: Short accepted certificates exist exactly for satisfiable circuits

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output, and let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ be an array of truth values, where an entry at a position at or beyond $m$ is read as false and the position of a wire is $k$ for input $k$ and $n + j$ for gate $j$. If the Boolean certificate verifier accepts $b$, then, writing $x = (b_0, \dots, b_{n-1})$, the value of every wire of $c$ on…
nodes.title: Soundness of the Boolean certificate verifier

nodes.summary: Let $K$ be a natural number and let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output in which every gate has at most $K$ arguments. Then for every array $b$ of truth values, the cost counted by the Boolean certificate verifier on $b$ is at most $2 + (K + 1)s$.
nodes.title: Linear cost of the Boolean certificate verifier

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output, and let $b$ be an array of $m$ truth values. The cost counted by the Boolean certificate verifier on $b$ is $2 + s + \sum_{j < s} a_j$ if $m = n + s$, where $a_j$ is the number of arguments of gate $j$, and $1$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Cost of the Boolean certificate verifier

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a circuit over the Boolean signature with $n$ inputs, $s$ gates and one output, and let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ be an array of truth values, read as a value for each wire: input $k$ at position $k$ and gate $j$ at position $n + j$. The verifier is a computation with a counted cost. It first checks whether $m = n + s$, at cost $1$; if not, it returns false. Otherwise, for each gate $j < s$ in order,…
nodes.title: Boolean certificate verifier

nodes.summary: An instance $(n, G)$ with gates $G = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ is well formed when every gate $g_j = (o, a, b)$ satisfies $o \le 5$, and moreover: if $o = 0$ or $o = 1$ then $a < n + j$ and $b < n + j$; if $o = 2$ then $a < n + j$; and if $o = 3$ then $a < n$.
nodes.title: Well-formed circuit-satisfiability instances

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
